item.title: “Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? Form, monks, is…
item.description:
“Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? Form, monks, is not yours — abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. Feeling … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is not yours — abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.33

item.title: “Good, Māgandiya. I too have never seen or heard of such a one. But, Māgandiya, those ascetics or brahmins who have dwelt, dwell, or will…
item.description:
“Good, Māgandiya. I too have never seen or heard of such a one. But, Māgandiya, those ascetics or brahmins who have dwelt, dwell, or will dwell with craving cut off and mind inwardly peaceful—all of them, having known as they actually are the origination, the passing away, the gratification, the peril, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, with craving for sensual pleasures abandoned and the fever of sensual pleasures removed, have dwelt, dwell, or will dwell with craving cut off and mind inwardly peaceful.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 75 – Māgandiyasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, if a monk lives without ardor in his practice, though he may wish: ‘May my mind be liberated from the defilements without clinging,’ yet…
item.description:
“Monks, if a monk lives without ardor in his practice, though he may wish: ‘May my mind be liberated from the defilements without clinging,’ yet his mind is not liberated from the defilements without clinging. Why is that? It is because he has not developed. Not developed what? He has not developed the four foundations of mindfulness. He has not developed the four right efforts. He has not developed the four bases of spiritual power. He has not developed the five faculties. He has not developed the five powers. He has not developed the seven factors of enlightenment. He has not developed the Noble Eightfold Path.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.101
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, dwell contemplating foulness in the body. Establish well mindfulness of breathing, setting mindfulness before you, inwardly directed. Dwell contemplating impermanence in all conditioned things.…
item.description:
“Monks, dwell contemplating foulness in the body. Establish well mindfulness of breathing, setting mindfulness before you, inwardly directed. Dwell contemplating impermanence in all conditioned things. For one dwelling contemplating foulness in the body, the underlying tendency to lust for the beautiful is abandoned. For one who has well-established mindfulness of breathing, setting mindfulness before you, inwardly directed, there are no externally directed, harmful thoughts. For one dwelling contemplating impermanence in all conditioned things, ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge arises.

Contemplating foulness in the body,
Mindful of in-breath and out-breath,
Calming all conditioned things,
Ever ardent, right in view —

That monk who sees rightly,
From that, being thus liberated,
Perfects direct knowledge,
Is at peace, truly stilled —
That sage has certainly crossed beyond all yokes.”

From: Itivuttaka 85

item.title: “And what, monks, is right effort? Here, monks, a monk awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is right effort? Here, monks, a monk awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states. He awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states. He awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states. He awakens desire, makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the continuance, non-disappearance, strengthening, increase, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states. This, monks, is called right effort.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.8
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, thought: ‘This Dhamma that I have realized is deep, hard to see, hard to…
item.description:
“Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, thought: ‘This Dhamma that I have realized is deep, hard to see, hard to awaken to, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of logic, subtle, to be understood by the wise. But this generation delights in sensual pleasures, is devoted to sensual pleasures, is fond of sensual pleasures. For a generation that delights in sensual pleasures, is devoted to sensual pleasures, is fond of sensual pleasures, it is hard to see this principle of specific conditionality (dependent origination); it is hard to see the principle that all formations are peaceful, that all substrates of rebirth are eliminated, that craving is destroyed, that there is dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 14 – Mahāpadānasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, with guarded faculties, with completeness in guarding the faculties, virtue is complete. With virtue present, with completeness in virtue, right concentration is complete. With…
item.description:
“Monks, with guarded faculties, with completeness in guarding the faculties, virtue is complete. With virtue present, with completeness in virtue, right concentration is complete. With right concentration present, with completeness in right concentration, true knowledge and vision are complete. With true knowledge and vision present, with completeness in true knowledge and vision, disenchantment and dispassion are complete. With disenchantment and dispassion present, with completeness in disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation are complete. Just as, monks, a tree with complete branches and foliage — its shoots reach perfection, its bark reaches perfection, its sapwood reaches perfection, its heartwood reaches perfection. So too, monks, with guarded faculties, with completeness in guarding the faculties … the knowledge and vision of liberation are complete.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.50

item.title: Having abandoned sensual desires in the world, Homeless, gone forth into renunciation, Having abandoned sensual desire and existence, That one I call a true brahmin.…
item.description:
Having abandoned sensual desires in the world,
Homeless, gone forth into renunciation,
Having abandoned sensual desire and existence,
That one I call a true brahmin.

Having abandoned greed and ill-will in the world,
Homeless, gone forth into renunciation,
Having abandoned ill-will and existence,
That one I call a true brahmin.

Who has abandoned the human yoke
And transcended the heavenly yoke,
Having abandoned all yokes,
Released from all bondage —
That one I call a true brahmin.

Having abandoned pleasure and displeasure,
Cooled, without substratum,
A hero who has conquered all worlds,
Mighty and courageous —
That one I call a true brahmin.

Who fully and truly knows
The passing away and rebirth of beings,
Not clinging, well-gone, awakened,
Attained to perfect enlightenment —
That one I call a true brahmin.

Who has no clinging to the past,
The future, or the present,
Not clinging, without possessions —
That one I call a true brahmin.

Who knows his former abodes,
Sees heavenly and evil destinations,
And has attained the destruction of birth —
That one I call a true brahmin.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 98 – Vāseṭṭhasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Elder Siṅgālapitar: “Look at the forest of Bhesakaḷā! A monk lives there, Heir to the Buddha’s teaching, Pervading this great earth With the perception of…
item.description:
Elder Siṅgālapitar:
“Look at the forest of Bhesakaḷā!
A monk lives there,
Heir to the Buddha’s teaching,
Pervading this great earth
With the perception of a skeleton.
I think that monk will quickly
Abandon sensual lust.”

From: Theragāthā 1.18

item.title: Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having personally abandoned discontent and aroused satisfaction, on that occasion recited this verse: I abandon pleasure and displeasure, All household thoughts,…
item.description:
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having personally abandoned discontent and aroused satisfaction, on that occasion recited this verse:

I abandon pleasure and displeasure,
All household thoughts,
Making no place anywhere
That could become a basis for sensual desire.
One who has escaped the forest of greed,
Escaped all sensual desire,
Free from greed, not clinging —
He is truly called a monk.
Whatever earth element, space element,
All the form realm in the world —
All things are subject to change,
All things are impermanent.
Whoever understands this,
His conduct is true.
Beings are always attached
To various attachments —
To what they see, hear,
Smell, taste, touch.
Whoever abandons desire here,
With mind undefiled,
Not clinging here or there —
He is called a sage (muni).
Concerning the sixty views
Belonging to wrong thoughts —
Worldlings cling to them,
Grasp and cling.
The monk who has no defilements,
Speaks no evil words,
Clear-minded, always concentrated,
Without deceit, careful —
Escaped from all craving.
The sage who has attained
The peaceful state of Nibbāna,
Awaiting the time of his end,
With mind perfectly still,
Serenely passes into Nibbāna.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 8.2
📖 Read this sutta
